messages.content: I want to develop semantic parsers that generalize to unseen operator compositions, even when training contains correlations between linguistic templates and program structure. What does that goal require?

It has two requirements. On held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations, the parsers should achieve 80% exact-match accuracy. At the same time, their in-distribution exact-match accuracy should remain within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. The aim is therefore not only to handle the held-out compositions, but to do so without substantially changing the in-distribution result relative to that comparator.
What is the concern about correlations between linguistic templates and program structure?

A parser could appear to understand a request while relying heavily on a familiar pairing between how the request is phrased and the structure of its target program. If that pairing changes, the familiar phrasing may no longer be a dependable guide to structure. The goal is for parsing to carry over to unseen combinations of operators despite those training correlations. That describes the generalization challenge; it does not assert that any particular parser has failed for that reason.
So is the held-out condition simply unfamiliar wording?

Not simply. The stated condition concerns unseen operator compositions and reversed template–structure correlations. Wording matters because linguistic templates are part of the correlation, but the target is exact matching of the resulting program on compositions that were held out. Describing the test as only unfamiliar wording would leave out the program-composition requirement and the reversal condition.
Can you clarify what 'reversed template–structure correlations' adds?

It makes the correlation encountered during training an unreliable shortcut for the held-out condition: the relationship between templates and structures is reversed. The point is to assess whether the parser can produce the appropriate program structure rather than merely reproduce a template–structure association. The goal does not specify the particular templates, operators, or reversal procedure.
And what exactly is being measured by the 80% figure?

It is the exact-match accuracy target on held-out operator compositions under those reversed template–structure correlations. Exact match concerns whether the predicted program matches the target program, rather than whether it is approximately similar. The 80% figure applies to that held-out condition, not to the in-distribution comparison.
Could strong performance on the held-out condition alone satisfy the whole goal?

No. The in-distribution requirement is separate: exact-match accuracy there must stay within two percentage points of the accuracy of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. The goal asks for both properties together. Reaching the held-out target while falling outside that in-distribution comparison would not meet the full stated objective.
Why specify an identically sized comparator?

It fixes the size comparison for the in-distribution requirement. The reference is not just any conventionally trained parser; it is one of identical size. The goal gives no particular size or measured accuracy for that parser, so the two-percentage-point condition is a relative criterion rather than a stated in-distribution score.
Does 'within two percentage points' mean a two percent relative difference?

No. Percentage points compare accuracy percentages directly; they are not a relative percentage change. The requirement is that the two in-distribution exact-match accuracy figures differ by no more than two percentage points. It should not be read as permission for a gap equal to two percent of the comparator's score.
Is the conventionally trained parser also the reference for the held-out 80% target?

The wording assigns it a specific role in the in-distribution comparison. The held-out requirement is stated as an 80% exact-match target for the parsers being developed. It does not give the conventional parser a held-out score or require a particular held-out margin over that parser.
Does this already prescribe a way to train the new parsers?

No. It states the development goal and the two performance requirements, but not an architecture, training intervention, or implementation decision. The training correlations identify the challenge the parsers must withstand; they do not, by themselves, specify how to build parsers that withstand it.
Could I restate the goal as avoiding any use of linguistic templates?

That would be stronger than what is stated. Linguistic templates are part of the input-side information, and the goal does not prohibit using them. The concern is reliance on their training correlation with program structure in a way that prevents generalization when that correlation is reversed. The desired outcome is accurate parsing of unseen operator compositions under that condition, while retaining the specified in-distribution accuracy.
How should I keep the two evaluation conditions distinct when I describe the goal?

Name the metric in each case, then attach its own condition. First: 80% exact-match accuracy on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations. Second: in-distribution exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. Both use exact match, but they apply to different conditions, and only the second is expressed relative to the comparator.
Does this say that such a parser has already achieved either result?

No. 'Develop' and 'achieve' express an objective. Neither an observed 80% held-out score nor an observed in-distribution comparison is supplied. Those figures are requirements for the intended parsers, not reports of completed results.
Then the central tension is generalizing beyond the template–structure correlations without losing more than two percentage points in-distribution relative to the same-size conventional parser?

Yes, with the held-out target made explicit: the intended parsers should reach 80% exact-match accuracy on unseen operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations, while keeping in-distribution exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. That states the two requirements together without assuming a particular method or a result already obtained.
What approach would you propose for the semantic parser goal?

I would propose training SwapParse with operator-aligned counterfactual template swaps and compositional decoding, alongside in-distribution distillation from a same-size baseline. The swaps and decoding are intended to address generalization when familiar template–structure correlations do not hold; the in-distribution distillation is intended to help preserve performance on the familiar distribution. This is a training proposal, not a claim that SwapParse has met either accuracy requirement.
What does the name SwapParse refer to here?

SwapParse is the proposed parser to train. The defining elements named in the proposal are operator-aligned counterfactual template swaps, compositional decoding, and in-distribution distillation from a same-size baseline. The name itself does not specify an architecture or establish any measured result.
Can you unpack 'operator-aligned counterfactual template swaps' without assuming a particular implementation?

The phrase indicates swaps of linguistic templates considered in relation to the operators they express. 'Operator-aligned' matters because the proposal is about learning to parse operator compositions, not merely changing wording indiscriminately. 'Counterfactual' indicates presenting a different template–operator association than the familiar training correlation would suggest. The proposal does not give a concrete swap procedure or specify which templates or operators are involved.
Why include swaps if compositional decoding is already part of the proposal?

They play different proposed roles. Template swaps address what associations the parser encounters during training: they are meant to reduce dependence on a fixed pairing of linguistic form and program structure. Compositional decoding addresses how the parser produces a program: it emphasizes putting together operator-level structure. Neither element, as stated, guarantees generalization on its own; the proposal combines them.
Does 'operator-aligned' mean any template can be attached to any program?

No. The qualifier points away from unrestricted rearrangement: the swaps are to be aligned with operators. Beyond that, the proposal does not spell out eligibility rules for swaps or a method for checking alignment. Claiming that arbitrary templates can be attached to arbitrary programs would go beyond what is stated.
What should I understand by compositional decoding in this context?

Conceptually, it means decoding a program in a way that treats its operator composition as meaningful, rather than depending solely on a familiar whole-template-to-whole-program association. That matches the aim of parsing unseen operator compositions. The proposal does not specify the decoder's architecture, its intermediate representations, or a particular decoding algorithm.
And the distillation component is specifically in-distribution?

Yes. The proposal calls for in-distribution distillation from a same-size baseline. Its intended role is to help SwapParse retain in-distribution parsing behavior while the other components target robustness to the template–structure correlation. Nothing in the proposal says that distillation is applied to the held-out condition or gives its precise training objective.
Is the same-size baseline necessarily the exact comparator mentioned in the accuracy goal?

The proposal specifies a same-size baseline as the source for distillation. The goal separately specifies an identically sized, conventionally trained parser for the in-distribution accuracy comparison. Size is explicit in both descriptions, but the proposal does not expressly say that its distillation baseline and the evaluation comparator are the same trained parser. It is safest not to add that identification.
Would the distillation erase the benefit of the swaps?

That is a reasonable question about the proposed combination, but the node provides no result that resolves it. The intended balance is for the swaps and compositional decoding to support generalization while in-distribution distillation supports retention of familiar-distribution accuracy. Whether those aims coexist successfully would have to be established rather than assumed.
So which part speaks to the reversed template–structure correlations?

Most directly, the operator-aligned counterfactual template swaps are aimed at making the familiar correlation less decisive during training. Compositional decoding complements that by emphasizing the operator composition in the output. Together they are proposed as a response to the held-out condition with reversed template–structure correlations; the proposal does not claim that their effect has already been measured.
Which part speaks to the two-percentage-point in-distribution condition?

The in-distribution distillation from a same-size baseline is the part explicitly aimed at retaining in-distribution behavior. The requirement itself is that in-distribution exact-match accuracy remain within two percentage points of an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. The distillation is a proposed way to pursue that requirement, not evidence that the gap is already within two percentage points.
Could we describe SwapParse as solving the 80% held-out target?

Not yet. The 80% exact-match accuracy on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations is a target from the goal. SwapParse is a proposed training approach meant to pursue it. No held-out accuracy for SwapParse is given.
What if I say the swaps directly teach every unseen composition?

That would overstate the proposal. The swaps are proposed to counter reliance on template–structure correlations, and compositional decoding is proposed to support combining operators. The node does not claim that the training process covers every held-out composition or directly supplies the answer for each one. Generalization to unseen compositions remains the intended outcome.
Is it accurate to call this three separate training methods?

It is more accurate to describe one proposed approach with three specified components: training SwapParse using operator-aligned counterfactual template swaps and compositional decoding, with in-distribution distillation from a same-size baseline. Calling them three unrelated methods would obscure their proposed joint purpose.
Please put the proposal in one sentence without suggesting it has already worked.

Propose training SwapParse with operator-aligned counterfactual template swaps and compositional decoding, while using in-distribution distillation from a same-size baseline to help retain familiar-distribution accuracy as it pursues generalization to unseen operator compositions.
What fraction of SwapParse template swaps preserve operator scope in nested negation–quantifier utterances?

I can’t give a numerical fraction from the information available. The question asks, among SwapParse template swaps involving nested negation–quantifier utterances, how many preserve the intended scope of those operators. No count of qualifying swaps or count of scope-preserving swaps has been provided.
What would the numerator and denominator be?

The denominator would be the SwapParse template swaps in the specified nested negation–quantifier utterances. The numerator would be the swaps among them that preserve operator scope. Dividing the numerator by the denominator would give the fraction, once those counts and the criterion for preservation are established.
Why focus on scope rather than just whether the swapped utterance still contains negation and a quantifier?

Because retaining both operators does not necessarily retain their relationship. Operator scope concerns how the negation and quantifier are composed: which takes effect within the other’s reach. A swap could keep the same operator words while changing that relationship. The question is specifically about preserving scope, not merely preserving the presence of the operators.
Does the question tell us which scope relationship the utterances are supposed to have?

No. It identifies nested negation–quantifier utterances but does not specify an intended nesting order for any particular utterance. Scope preservation would have to be assessed relative to the intended operator structure for each relevant case; I should not assume one ordering applies to them all.
Could the answer be inferred from the fact that the template swaps are operator-aligned?

No. 'Operator-aligned' describes the proposed swaps, but it does not supply a measured scope-preservation rate. In particular, alignment with operators does not by itself tell us whether every swap preserves their scope when negation and a quantifier are nested. That is precisely what the question is asking about.
Is this asking about SwapParse’s parsing accuracy?

Not directly. It asks for a fraction of template swaps that preserve operator scope in a particular kind of utterance. That concerns a property of the swaps. Parsing accuracy would concern whether predicted programs exactly match their targets; no parsing-accuracy result for this subset is given here.
If one swapped utterance is ambiguous, can we automatically count it as scope-preserving?

The question does not specify a rule for ambiguous utterances, so an automatic answer would be unwarranted. To report a fraction, 'preserve operator scope' would need a consistent interpretation for the swaps being counted. Without that criterion, even the numerator may be uncertain.
Would it be fair to report a percentage instead of a fraction?

A percentage could express the same quantity after multiplying the fraction by 100, but neither can be calculated without the relevant counts. The key point is to keep the denominator restricted to SwapParse template swaps in nested negation–quantifier utterances, rather than all template swaps or all utterances.
So what is the most precise answer we can give right now?

The fraction is not specified. It would be the number of SwapParse template swaps in nested negation–quantifier utterances that preserve operator scope, divided by the total number of SwapParse template swaps in that specified set. The available information supplies neither count nor a scope-preservation judgment for individual swaps.
For the scope-preservation question, I want to state a hypothesis: at least 95% of operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps preserve gold scope on nested negation–quantifier utterances.

That is a specific hypothesis about the swaps: among operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps on nested negation–quantifier utterances, the fraction that preserve gold scope is at least 95%. It gives a proposed answer to the fraction question, but it is not an observed result.
What does 'gold scope' add to the wording?

It identifies the reference for deciding whether scope is preserved. The question is not just whether a swapped utterance still includes a negation and a quantifier; it is whether their scope relationship remains consistent with the gold, or intended, scope. The hypothesis does not specify a particular scope ordering for every utterance.
Does the 95% refer to all SwapParse template swaps?

No. The stated population is operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps on nested negation–quantifier utterances. Broadening the claim to all SwapParse swaps, or to other kinds of utterances, would change the hypothesis.
If the fraction were exactly 95%, would the hypothesis hold?

Yes. 'At least 95%' includes exactly 95%. Equivalently, within the specified population, the hypothesis allows no more than 5% of swaps to fail to preserve gold scope. That is just another way of expressing the threshold, not a measured failure rate.
Is this a hypothesis about how accurately SwapParse predicts programs?

No. It concerns whether the operator-aligned template swaps preserve gold scope in the specified utterances. Parser exact-match accuracy is a different quantity: it concerns predicted programs matching target programs. A high scope-preservation fraction for swaps would not, by itself, establish a particular parsing-accuracy score.
But the swaps are operator-aligned. Why not say they all preserve scope?

Operator alignment is part of how the swaps are described, but it does not entail perfect scope preservation in nested negation–quantifier utterances. The hypothesis sets the threshold at at least 95%, rather than asserting 100%. Whether the threshold is actually reached remains unknown from the information given.
How does this answer the earlier question about a fraction?

It proposes a bound on that fraction, with an explicit restriction to operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps and an explicit criterion of preserving gold scope. It does not provide a measured numerator, denominator, or calculated fraction. So it addresses what the fraction might be, while leaving its actual value to be determined.
Could I phrase it as '95% of nested negation–quantifier utterances preserve scope'?

That would shift what is being counted. The hypothesis counts operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps on those utterances, and asks what fraction of those swaps preserve gold scope. Utterances themselves are not the stated denominator.
What if an utterance has more than one possible interpretation of the negation and quantifier?

The word 'gold' still makes the intended reference central: preservation is relative to the gold scope for the case in question. The hypothesis does not say how gold scope is assigned or how any ambiguity is handled. Those details cannot be filled in merely from the at-least-95% claim.
Does 'preserve' mean the swapped utterance must keep the exact same words?

No. These are template swaps, so preserving the exact wording is not what the hypothesis states. It is the gold scope relationship among the nested operators that must be preserved. Wording can be different without necessarily changing that relationship, just as familiar words could remain while the scope relationship changes.
Can we conclude that the proposed training approach will meet the held-out accuracy target if this hypothesis holds?

No. Gold-scope preservation by swaps concerns one property of the proposed training material. The held-out goal concerns exact-match accuracy on unseen operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations. The hypothesis does not claim that meeting its 95% threshold is sufficient for that accuracy target.
Nor does it establish the in-distribution comparison, right?

Right. The at-least-95% hypothesis does not report in-distribution exact-match accuracy or its difference from an identically sized, conventionally trained parser. It should remain a claim about gold-scope preservation for the specified swaps, not be recast as evidence that either broader performance requirement has been achieved.
What is the cleanest one-sentence formulation?
The hypothesis is that at least 95% of operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps preserve gold scope on nested negation–quantifier utterances.
How would we measure whether the SwapParse swaps preserve scope in nested negation–quantifier utterances?

The planned activity is to blindly annotate operator scope for 400 nested negation–quantifier SwapParse swaps, then compare those annotations with the source programs to measure preservation. This is a plan for obtaining the measurement, not a reported preservation fraction.
What are we annotating: the swapped utterance or the source program?

The annotation concerns the operator scope expressed by each swapped utterance. The source program is the reference used afterward for comparison. That distinction matters because the question is whether the swap still expresses the source program’s scope, not simply what scope the program contains.
Why make the scope annotation blind?

Blind annotation is intended to keep the interpretation of the swapped utterance separate from the answer supplied by its source program. Otherwise, knowledge of the program could influence what scope an annotator reads into the utterance. The activity does not specify a fuller blinding protocol, such as exactly what other information annotators would or would not see.
So should the source programs be consulted while the utterances are being annotated?

That would undermine the distinction in the stated activity: first blindly annotate scope, then compare with source programs. The comparison is how preservation is measured after the scope interpretation has been recorded. The plan does not provide additional procedural details beyond that sequence.
What does the comparison tell us for an individual swap?

It tells us whether the scope annotated for the swapped utterance agrees with the scope represented by its source program. Agreement would count toward scope preservation; disagreement would not. The relevant feature is the nesting relationship between negation and the quantifier, rather than merely the presence of both operators.
Would 400 be the numerator of the reported fraction?

No. The activity specifies 400 swaps to annotate. If all 400 yield assessable comparisons, they form the denominator; the numerator is the number whose annotated scope agrees with their source programs. The activity supplies the planned number of swaps, not the number that will agree.
Could we calculate a preservation percentage now because we know the sample size?

No. Knowing that 400 swaps are to be annotated tells us how many cases the plan calls for, but not how many preserve scope. A percentage requires the comparison outcomes. No annotations or outcomes are reported in this node.
How does this relate to the at-least-95% scope-preservation hypothesis?

The planned measurement can be used to examine that hypothesis: it produces a preservation fraction to compare with the proposed at-least-95% threshold. The hypothesis is specifically about operator-aligned SwapParse template swaps, while the activity describes 400 nested negation–quantifier SwapParse swaps without expressly stating their selection criteria. The description alone therefore does not establish whether every annotated swap falls within that narrower population.
If the comparison were made against the original utterance instead, would that be the same activity?

No. The specified comparison is with the source programs. Comparing two utterances might be informative in another setting, but it would not replace the stated check of whether the swapped utterance’s annotated operator scope agrees with the program that serves as its reference.
Do the annotations need to reproduce every detail of each source program?

The stated annotation target is operator scope, and the comparison is for measuring scope preservation. The activity does not call for reconstructing or judging every aspect of each program. A swap could be discussed in terms of the scope relationship relevant here without this plan making claims about all its other properties.
What if a swapped utterance does not have a clear scope reading?

The plan does not say how ambiguous or unassessable readings would be handled. That matters for the eventual fraction, since a consistent rule would be needed to decide whether such a case contributes to the numerator or denominator. I would not assume a rule or a count of such cases from the activity as stated.
Does 'blindly annotate' tell us how many annotators there are or how disagreements are resolved?

No. It specifies blinding for the scope annotation, but gives no annotator count, agreement procedure, or adjudication rule. Those details should not be presented as though they are already part of the plan.
Is this an evaluation of SwapParse’s exact-match parsing accuracy?

No. It measures whether 400 SwapParse swaps preserve operator scope in nested negation–quantifier utterances by comparing blind scope annotations with source programs. Exact-match parsing accuracy would require comparing parser predictions with target programs; this activity does not report such predictions or scores.
What is the most precise description of the activity without adding procedures we have not specified?

Blindly annotate operator scope for 400 nested negation–quantifier SwapParse swaps, and compare the annotations with the corresponding source programs to measure how often scope is preserved. The number of preserving swaps—and thus the measured fraction—remains to be determined.
What did the blind annotation find for the SwapParse swaps?
It found that 386 of 400 SwapParse swaps preserved gold negation–quantifier scope. That is 96.5% of the annotated swaps.
Can you show how the percentage follows from the count?
Dividing 386 by 400 gives 0.965. Expressed as a percentage, that is 96.5%. The denominator is the 400 swaps examined through blind annotation, not every SwapParse swap.
What happened with the other swaps?

Fourteen of the 400 were not counted as preserving gold negation–quantifier scope: 400 minus 386 equals 14. The result does not describe those individual cases or say why they were not counted as preserving scope.
Does preserving scope mean the swapped utterance used the same words as its source?

No. The finding concerns the scope relationship between negation and the quantifier, assessed against the gold scope. It does not require identical wording, and it does not report a measure of wording similarity.
Why is the word 'gold' important in stating the result?

It specifies the reference for the preservation judgment. The 386 cases were counted because their annotated negation–quantifier scope preserved the gold scope, not merely because an annotator could identify some scope reading or find both operators in the utterance.
What does the result tell us about nested negation–quantifier utterances specifically?

The blind annotation concerned 400 SwapParse swaps of that kind. For those annotated swaps, 386 preserved the gold relationship in scope between negation and the quantifier. The result is scoped to that measurement; it does not give a rate for other kinds of utterances.
Can I describe 96.5% as SwapParse’s parsing accuracy?

No. It is the observed fraction of annotated swaps that preserved gold negation–quantifier scope. Parsing accuracy would measure whether a parser’s predicted programs match target programs. This finding does not report parser predictions or exact-match accuracy.
Does the figure establish that all SwapParse template swaps preserve operator scope?
No. Within the 400 annotated swaps, 386 were counted as preserving gold scope, not all 400. The figure also does not provide a preservation rate for all possible SwapParse swaps.
Is the 96.5% an estimate we need to calculate, or an observed result?

It is the percentage calculated from the reported blind-annotation result: 386 preserving swaps out of 400 examined. One can discuss what that observation might imply more broadly, but the stated evidence itself is the observed count and its corresponding percentage.
Does the result identify which template swaps failed to preserve scope?
No. It gives the aggregate result—386 of 400, or 96.5%, preserved gold negation–quantifier scope—without listing individual swaps or describing the non-preserving cases.
How should I state the finding without making a broader claim?
Blind annotation found that 386 of 400 SwapParse swaps, or 96.5%, preserved gold negation–quantifier scope.
What should we do with the operator-aligned SwapParse swaps?

Proceed with the operator-aligned SwapParse swaps, while filtering scope-ambiguous samples. The stated reason for proceeding is that audited preservation reached 96.5%. This is a decision about using the swaps with that filter, not a claim that every swap preserves scope.
Why proceed rather than set the swaps aside?

The decision explicitly rests on the audited 96.5% preservation figure. It treats that result as a reason to proceed with operator-aligned swaps, while still calling for scope-ambiguous samples to be filtered. It does not say that the figure eliminates every concern about individual samples.
Does filtering mean we only proceed with samples whose scope is completely unambiguous?

The decision says to filter scope-ambiguous samples, but it does not define a formal ambiguity test or a degree of certainty required for inclusion. The key distinction is to avoid carrying ambiguous scope readings forward as though their intended operator relationship were clear.
Are scope-ambiguous samples necessarily the ones that failed to preserve gold scope?

Not necessarily. Ambiguity and failure to preserve gold scope are different descriptions: an utterance could have an unclear scope reading, whereas a clearly read utterance could express a scope different from the intended one. The decision does not identify the filtered samples with any particular set of non-preserving swaps.
So does the 96.5% apply after filtering?

The wording gives 96.5% as the audited preservation figure motivating the decision. It does not report a new preservation percentage for the set remaining after scope-ambiguous samples are filtered. We should not present it as a post-filter measurement.
Is the filtering a replacement for keeping the swaps operator-aligned?

No. Both parts belong to the decision: proceed with operator-aligned SwapParse swaps and filter scope-ambiguous samples. Operator alignment describes the swaps being used; the filter addresses ambiguity about scope in samples. Neither part is stated as replacing the other.
Does this establish that SwapParse now reaches the held-out exact-match goal?

No. The 96.5% figure concerns audited scope preservation, and the decision concerns how to proceed with the swaps. It does not report exact-match accuracy on held-out operator compositions under reversed template–structure correlations.
What about in-distribution exact-match accuracy relative to the same-size conventional parser?

That comparison is not reported by this decision either. Proceeding with filtered operator-aligned swaps because audited preservation reached 96.5% says nothing by itself about the in-distribution exact-match gap.
Can I say that filtering guarantees preservation of gold scope in every retained sample?

No. Filtering scope-ambiguous samples is part of the decision, but no guarantee of perfect preservation for the retained swaps is stated. Nor is there a measured preservation rate for that retained set here.
Does the decision specify how many samples the filter will remove?

No. It does not provide a count or fraction of scope-ambiguous samples, a filtering procedure, or a resulting sample size. Those details should not be inferred from the 96.5% audited preservation figure.
How do I convey both the decision and its rationale in one sentence?
Proceed with operator-aligned SwapParse swaps, filtering scope-ambiguous samples, because audited preservation reached 96.5%.
What is the next plan for checking scope preservation in the SwapParse swaps?

Filter out scope-ambiguous swaps first. Then audit 200 swaps per negation–quantifier ordering and report gold-scope preservation after filtering. The plan specifies that sequence and the audit count for each ordering; it does not yet provide a post-filter result.
Why does the order of those steps matter?

Because the requested measurement is post-filter gold-scope preservation. Filtering first defines the set of swaps eligible for that measurement. Auditing before filtering would answer a different question unless the results were subsequently restricted to swaps that passed the filter.
When you say 200 per ordering, is 200 the total audit size?

No. It is 200 swaps for each negation–quantifier ordering. The plan does not state a single overall audit total or enumerate the orderings, so I would not replace '200 per ordering' with an unsupported total.
What does it mean to distinguish the orderings?

The relevant distinction is how negation and the quantifier are ordered in the operator-scope relationship. Auditing per ordering keeps the planned count attached to each such relationship, rather than treating all nested negation–quantifier swaps as one undifferentiated set. The plan does not list particular utterances or define a classification procedure.
Is this an audit of utterances, programs, or swaps?
The specified unit is the swap: 200 swaps per negation–quantifier ordering. The audit concerns whether those swaps preserve gold scope. The plan does not provide a more detailed audit protocol.
What exactly should the reported figure describe?

It should describe gold-scope preservation among swaps audited after scope-ambiguous swaps have been filtered. In other words, the reported outcome concerns the retained swaps, not an unfiltered collection. No numerical post-filter preservation figure is supplied yet.
Would the audit count scope-ambiguous swaps as failures?
Not as the plan is worded. It calls for filtering scope-ambiguous swaps before auditing 200 swaps per ordering. It does not specify how many swaps will be filtered or assign them an audit outcome.
Does filtering ambiguous swaps mean every retained swap must preserve gold scope?

No. A swap can have a clear scope reading and still fail to preserve the gold scope. Filtering ambiguity addresses whether scope can be read clearly; the subsequent audit addresses whether the scope that is read agrees with the gold scope. The plan does not guarantee the audit’s outcome.
Are we supposed to report a separate preservation percentage for each ordering?

The plan explicitly requires auditing 200 swaps per ordering and reporting post-filter gold-scope preservation. That structure makes preservation within each ordering assessable, but it does not specify the exact format of the report or say that only separate percentages, only a combined percentage, or both must be reported.
Could one ordering contribute fewer than 200 audited swaps if the filter removes many?

The planned audit size remains 200 swaps per ordering after filtering. The plan does not say how many candidate swaps are available or what would happen if too few remain. It would be premature to assume either that this difficulty will occur or how it would be handled.
Does the plan say how to identify scope ambiguity?
No. It instructs us to filter scope-ambiguous swaps but does not define an ambiguity criterion or a filtering procedure. Those details should not be supplied as though they were already decided.
Does it specify whether the new audit will be blind?

No. This plan says to audit 200 swaps per negation–quantifier ordering after filtering. It does not specify blinding, the number of annotators, or how judgments will be made. Calling the planned audit blind would add a procedure that is not stated here.
If we report a fraction, what would be counted?

For an ordering, the numerator would be the audited, post-filter swaps found to preserve gold scope, and the denominator would be the swaps audited for that ordering—planned as 200. The actual numerator is unknown. The plan does not prescribe whether an overall fraction should also be reported.
Is the purpose to measure parsing exact-match accuracy as well?

No. The stated outcome is post-filter gold-scope preservation for swaps in the negation–quantifier orderings. It does not call for evaluating predicted programs or reporting exact-match parsing accuracy.
How can I state the plan concisely without implying that the audit has happened?
Filter scope-ambiguous SwapParse swaps, then audit 200 swaps per negation–quantifier ordering and report the resulting post-filter gold-scope preservation.
What is the activity for the SwapParse scope audit?

Apply scope-ambiguity filters to the SwapParse swaps, then blindly annotate 200 retained examples for each negation–quantifier ordering. The examples annotated are the ones retained after filtering. This describes the activity; it does not provide annotation outcomes or a post-filter preservation rate.
Does 'retained' mean the examples are chosen before the ambiguity filters are applied?

No. 'Retained' refers to examples that remain after the scope-ambiguity filters are applied. The stated sequence is filtering first, followed by blind annotation of 200 retained examples for each ordering.
What is the filter meant to remove?

It targets swaps whose scope is ambiguous. In this setting, the scope at issue is the relationship between negation and the quantifier. The activity does not specify an operational test for ambiguity or say how many swaps the filters remove.
If a swap passes the filter, does that establish that it preserves gold scope?
